content.title: About
content.content: Bean dip made with refried beans is a thick, flavorful sauce with a smooth bean base, seasoned with spices and sometimes enriched with cheese, lime or chili. It is used as a snack dip for chips and vegetables or as a filling for tacos and burritos.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally popular in Mexican cuisine, where it is known as “frijoles refritos” or “bean sauce”.
Refried beans are created by frying cooked beans with oil and spices, giving the dip its characteristic creamy texture.
Bean dip is often served hot, but it can also be enjoyed cold as a party dip.
Variations may include cheddar cheese, sour cream, guacamole or fresh cilantro.
The beans used are rich in plant protein and fiber.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide a high amount of protein, essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared dip often contains salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: Insufficiently heated dip may retain toxins that form when beans are not cooked properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve bean dip with tortilla chips, fresh vegetables, flatbreads, in tacos, burritos, or as a sauce for grilled dishes. Heat in the microwave or on the stovetop, adding a splash of water or broth to reach the desired consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, preferably portioned out beforehand.

chicken-or-turkey-noodles-and-vegetables.title: Chicken or Turkey with Noodles and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This dish combines tender chicken or turkey meat, boiled noodles, and a mix of vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. It is served without sauce, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein containing all essential amino acids.
Whole‑grain noodles supply complex carbohydrates for steady energy release.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support the body’s detox pathways.
Carrots contain beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables like spinach or kale are excellent sources of iron and folate.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Poultry meat offers easily digestible protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin richness
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 from the meat support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from broccoli and beta‑carotene from carrots boost the body’s immune defenses.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K from leafy greens help maintain strong bones.

items.title: Steady energy
items.content: Complex carbs in noodles provide lasting satiety and stable blood‑glucose levels.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑salted noodles can increase the dish’s sodium level.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High fiber from vegetables may cause discomfort in people with sensitive gastrointestinal tracts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing pieces of chicken or turkey with noodles and vegetables. Fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a drizzle of olive oil can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly until boiling to eliminate any possible bacteria.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are pre‑cooked pieces of poultry meat, fried to a golden crisp and ready to eat. The package includes wings coated with a variety of sauces or seasonings such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, spicy chili and garlic sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are a popular snack in bars and restaurants worldwide.
The classic American “Buffalo wings” are tossed in a buttery hot sauce.
Chicken wings are rich in collagen, which is beneficial for skin and joints.
A wide range of sauces makes it easy to match any taste preference—from sweet to very hot.
Wings freeze well; after thawing they retain juiciness thanks to the pre‑cooking process.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Wings provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: For low‑carb diets, wings are a good option, especially when paired with non‑sweet sauces.

items.title: Antioxidants in sauces
items.content: Spice blends often include garlic, paprika and ginger, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Spiciness of sauces
items.content: Very hot sauces may irritate the gastrointestinal tract and cause heartburn.

items.title: Thermal safety
items.content: Even though pre‑cooked, wings should be reheated to an internal temperature of 75 °C to prevent food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the wings hot; they are conveniently eaten with the hands, pulling the meat off the bone. Drizzle extra sauce, sprinkle fresh herbs, or pair with vegetable sticks and dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze; thaw in the fridge and then reheat in the oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Cappuccino is a popular coffee drink made from espresso, hot milk, and milk foam. In the nonfat version, low‑fat milk (usually 1–2 %) is used. The drink has a smooth, creamy taste and the characteristic aroma of roasted coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name cappuccino comes from the Italian “cappuccio” meaning “hood”, referring to the foam‑capped appearance.
Traditionally the drink follows a 1:1:1 ratio – one part espresso, one part hot milk, and one part foam.
The nonfat version appeared in the 1970s as consumers sought lower‑calorie options.
In Japan cappuccino is often served with a sweet soy bean paste called “anko”.
Cappuccino is frequently used as a base for flavored drinks – with cinnamon, vanilla or caramel.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cognitive function
items.content: Caffeine improves alertness, reaction time and short‑term memory.

items.title: May lower risk of certain diseases
items.content: Regular moderate coffee consumption is linked to a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes and some cancers.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using nonfat milk reduces the calorie content while still providing protein and calcium.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee provides niacin (B3), riboflavin (B2) and other B‑vitamins involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may enhance the effects of stimulants and diminish the efficacy of sedatives.

items.title: Possible calcium shortfall
items.content: Nonfat milk contains less calcium than whole milk, so additional calcium sources are advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cappuccino hot in a ceramic cup. Drink it soon after preparation to enjoy the aroma and foam texture. Sweeten with sugar, syrups or spices (cinnamon, nutmeg) if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store freshly roasted coffee beans in an airtight container in a cool, dark place, and keep milk refrigerated and use within 5 days. Use fresh ingredients for each preparation to preserve flavor and aroma.

double-hamburger-on-wheat-bun-2-large-pa.title: Double Hamburger on Wheat Bun, 2 Large Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double hamburger consists of a wheat bun, two large beef patties (about 85 g each), lettuce, a slice of tomato, pickles, onion, cheddar cheese and sauce. It is a classic fast‑food item popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first double hamburger appeared in the United States in the 1970s as a response to growing demand for heartier meals.
A wheat bun provides a softer texture compared with a standard white‑bread bun.
Each patty weighs roughly 85 g, making the total weight of the product about 250 g without toppings.
The combination of cheddar cheese and sauce gives a characteristic creamy flavor that intensifies when heated.
The burger is often served with french fries and a drink, forming a typical combo meal.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef patties are rich in complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat provides heme iron, which supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The burger contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheddar adds calcium, necessary for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: Lettuce and tomato contribute a modest amount of fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A double hamburger can contain 600–800 kcal, so it should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef patties and cheese contain saturated fats, which may raise cholesterol when consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauce and cheese add significant sodium, which can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheddar cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, split the bun, and layer the patties with the toppings. It is convenient to eat with hands, though a fork and knife can be used for a neater experience.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared burger in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in an oven or microwave to retain a crisp bun.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a small beef patty (1694), a bun, lettuce, tomato slice, cheese, sauce, and optional extra toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
There are more than 300 variations of hamburgers worldwide.
The world’s largest hamburger weighed over 1 ton.
In Japan, “rice burgers” replace the bun with compressed rice cakes.
The hamburger is often used as a symbol of American culture.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: High calories and fat
items.content: Large portions and added sauces can lead to overeating and weight gain.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef and cheese contain saturated fats, which may raise cholesterol when consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salty sauces and processed ingredients increase sodium intake, which can affect blood pressure.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The bun may contain gluten, and sauces often contain dairy, important for people with allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding the bottom bun. They are often served with fries, a dip, or a drink. For a healthier option, choose a whole‑grain bun and limit sauce amounts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared hamburger in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days in an airtight container. If needed, freeze for up to 2 months. Thaw in the fridge and reheat in an oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, soft quick‑bread typically made with flour, eggs, milk, butter, and a leavening agent. The oat bran version includes oat bran, which adds extra fiber and a subtle nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran is rich in soluble fiber and beta‑glucan, which support heart health.
Muffins are a popular snack served with tea or coffee.
They can be filled or topped with berries, nuts, chocolate, or cream cheese.
Bran makes muffins denser but still moist when the liquid ratio is balanced.
In the United States muffins are often marketed as a healthier alternative to cupcakes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oat bran provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Beta‑glucan can help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Bran muffins contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They supply magnesium, iron, and zinc, supporting muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The fiber slows sugar absorption, helping to maintain stable blood glucose.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional muffins contain wheat flour; people with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Despite the fiber, muffins remain calorie‑rich due to butter and sugar.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions can contribute to tooth decay and blood sugar spikes.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of bran may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a quick snack, split and spread with cream cheese or nut butter, added to yogurt, or used as a base for mini sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned oysters are a seafood product made from fresh oysters that are cleaned, lightly cooked, placed in airtight cans with brine or sauce, and then heat‑processed. Oysters are rich in minerals, vitamins, and protein, and canning preserves most of their nutritional value, allowing long‑term storage without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oysters can filter up to 50 liters of water per day, naturally cleaning their environment.
In ancient Rome, oysters were considered a luxury food and were even used as a form of currency.
Canning of oysters became widespread in the 19th century with the advent of tin cans and steam kettles.
While some oysters grow up to 30 cm, most canned varieties are small, about 5–7 cm in length.
Oysters contain more zinc per serving than beef, making them an excellent source of this mineral.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Oysters provide a high amount of zinc, which supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Source of omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and help reduce inflammation.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Easily digestible protein from oysters aids muscle building and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports thyroid function.

items.title: Allergy to shellfish
items.content: Oysters can trigger severe allergic reactions in people sensitive to shellfish.

items.title: Risk of contamination
items.content: Improper canning can allow bacterial growth that may cause foodborne illness.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned oysters often contain a lot of salt, so those with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Oysters are high in purines, which can be problematic for individuals with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned oysters can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, pasta, rice dishes, or used as a topping for toast. Before serving, drain the brine and, if desired, rinse briefly with cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the oysters refrigerated in their original container and consume within 3–4 days. Discard if the can is bulging, leaking, or the oysters develop an off‑odor.

peanut-butter-vitamin-and-mineral-fortif.title: Peanut Butter, Vitamin and Mineral Fortified

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter fortified with vitamins and minerals is made from roasted peanuts to which a blend of micronutrients (vitamins B‑complex, vitamin E, iron, zinc, etc.) is added to boost its nutritional value. It has a smooth, creamy texture, a characteristic nutty flavor, and can be used as a spread, cooking ingredient, or dietary supplement.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fortified peanut butter is especially popular in the United States and Canada, where it is often included in school meals.
The added vitamins and minerals help meet a portion of daily micronutrient requirements, useful for children and people with limited diets.
Although commonly called a nut, peanut is actually a legume.
Unlike many commercial peanut butters, fortified versions are usually free of added sugars and trans‑fats.
Manufacturers often use micro‑encapsulation technology to preserve vitamin stability during storage.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A serving provides about 7 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: These fats help maintain cardiovascular health and aid absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Fortified with B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B3 and B6 play key roles in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides vitamin E and selenium
items.content: These antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals: iron, zinc, magnesium
items.content: These minerals support immune function, blood formation, and muscle activity.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Individuals with peanut allergy may experience severe reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite its benefits, the spread is calorie‑dense, so portion control is important.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Some varieties contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Vitamin stability
items.content: Prolonged exposure to light and heat can degrade added vitamins; proper storage is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use fortified peanut butter as a spread on bread, stir it into smoothies, oatmeal, or yogurt, and incorporate it into sauces and baked goods. For children, offer small amounts and monitor for any allergic reaction.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, store in the refrigerator and consume within 2–3 months. Discard if it develops a rancid odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza rolls are bite‑size pieces of dough filled with sauce, cheese and typical pizza toppings such as sausage, ham or vegetables. They are baked in the oven or microwaved and serve as a snack or quick meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pizza rolls first appeared in the United States in the early 1990s as a convenient fast‑food option.
More than 20 filling varieties exist, including meat, vegetarian and even sweet versions.
They are often sold frozen, allowing long‑term storage.
In Japan, pizza rolls are popular with seafood and soy‑based sauces.
A typical serving is 5‑8 pieces, making them ideal for kids’ menus.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat, cheese or legume fillings provide protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and meat fillings are rich in B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate fiber
items.content: When vegetables are added, rolls can supply dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from the dough are rapidly absorbed, making rolls a handy pre‑exercise snack.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese and sauces often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meaty and cheesy fillings can be high in saturated fat, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Products may contain dairy, gluten and soy, common allergens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pizza rolls are relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is important for weight management.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: Rich cheese and fatty fillings can cause stomach heaviness in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat pizza rolls in a preheated oven at 180 °C for 5‑7 minutes or microwave for 30‑60 seconds. Serve with marinara, cheese sauce or spicy chili sauce. They are eaten by hand as a snack or added to salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen rolls in a freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, cook within 24 hours and store cooked rolls in the refrigerator for no more than 2‑3 days. Do not leave cooked rolls at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

potato-only-from-puerto-rican-mixed-dish.title: Potato only from Puerto Rican mixed dishes, gravy and other components

content.title: About
content.content: Potato is the tuber of the plant Solanum tuberosum. In Puerto Rico it is widely used in traditional dishes such as mofongo, arroz con pollo, and as a side to gravies. This product contains only the potato component, without meat, seafood or other additives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican potatoes are often grown on volcanic soils, giving them a distinctive flavor.
In Puerto Rico potato is a staple for many street foods and family meals.
Traditional mofongo includes plantains, pork and potatoes, but this product isolates the potato part only.
Potatoes are frequently served with a creamy sauce called "aguas fritas" made from milk and spices.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties worldwide; Puerto Rico favors short‑stalk types ideal for frying.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Potatoes contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Green spots and sprouts may contain the toxic compound solanine; these parts should be removed.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Foodborne illness from improper storage
items.content: Storing potatoes in warm, humid conditions can cause spoilage and toxin formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Potatoes can be boiled, baked, fried, or mashed. In Puerto Rican cuisine they are often served with a creamy garlic‑spice gravy, added to salads, or baked in casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store potatoes in a cool, dark, dry place, preferably in paper bags. Keep them away from onions, which accelerate sprouting. For longer storage, refrigerate but avoid moisture to prevent rot.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-eaten-mad.title: Potato, roasted, fresh, peel eaten, with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a tuber widely used in cooking. Roasted potatoes are made from fresh tubers that are peeled, sliced and fried in oil until golden. The peel remains edible, preserving additional nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
Roasted potatoes are one of the most popular side dishes worldwide.
The edible skin contains more fiber and vitamins than the flesh.
Frying creates a characteristic aroma through the Maillard reaction.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties differing in color and taste.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Roasted potatoes retain some vitamin C, which supports immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The skin adds fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Energy providing carbohydrates
items.content: Carbohydrates in potatoes quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Healthy fats from oil
items.content: Frying in vegetable oil adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for the heart.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying in oil increases calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Over‑cooking at high temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potential toxin.

items.title: Oil allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to the type of oil used.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large servings of fried potatoes may cause heaviness or indigestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served hot as a side dish, cut into wedges, sticks or cubes. They can be seasoned with salt, spices, herbs or cheese. The skin is left on to add crunch and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh tubers in a cool, dark place at 4–10 °C. Cooked roasted potatoes should be eaten within 2–3 days, kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness.
